Anthropic’s network and Congress

450 of 533

members of Congress have a tie on the public record to Anthropic’s network: 332 through something the network or the member did, 118 only through what third parties did. The network is the company, the funders behind it, the groups they fund, and their PACs and lobbyists.

Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026. A tie is a public record that links the member and the network: a contribution, a lobbying report on the member’s bill, a fellow in the office, a statement. The network, by one chain: Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna are the main funders of Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy); it awarded Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology $55.0M in 2019; that center’s witnesses have appeared before Congress 13 times.

Third parties are lobbyists at the network’s lobbying firms, who gave their own money, and super PACs that received network money and made their own expenditures. A tie can cut either way: a statement may be criticism, and a super PAC may have spent against the member. It is not an allegation, and a contribution is not a vote.

Start with the company: its employees’ own gifts, and its PAC’s.

What counts as a tie: the eleven kinds of record

A tie is one or more public records that link a member now serving and the network. Each count is the members with at least one record of that kind.

I · The arrival

At the end of 2024, 10 members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. By Sept. 30, 2026: 196.

The employees gave their own money: $5.6M, 92% of it dated 2026. The company’s PAC made its first gift on record to a member now serving on June 29, 2026; by Sept. 30 it had given $200K to 81 members, 18 of whom had no gift from an employee.

Source: FEC contribution records in this project’s tables: contributions to the campaign, leadership PAC or single-member joint fundraising committee of a serving member, through Sept. 30, 2026; ANTHROPAC is Anthropic PBC’s political action committee.

A person’s contribution is their own money, not their employer’s. Employer is as the giver reported it to the FEC. Both counts are of the members serving on Nov. 26, 2026; the record stops at Sept. 30, 2026.

Who gave it, and who received it?

Every gift on record to a member now serving: 1,027 from Anthropic’s employees, 87 from its PAC

Through Sept. 30, 2026. The scale is logarithmic: each line is ten times the one below. Dots are translucent, so a bright patch is many gifts of one size on nearby dates.

I · The arrival

Ten givers account for 58% of the employees’ dollars. Of the ten members who received the most, six are Republicans.

The filings list 89 distinct names with Anthropic as employer; half of them gave $20,500 or less. With the PAC’s gifts, Democrats received 55% of the dollars; Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, received the most.

A circle’s area is what one name as filed gave to members now serving; the smallest are drawn a little larger than scale. A member’s total counts campaign, leadership PAC and single-member joint fundraising committees.

Source: FEC contribution records; all years on record, through Sept. 30, 2026.

Givers are not named here; two people who share a first name and a surname count as one. A total is what the committees received, not what a member asked for. Republicans are more than half of the five largest recipients, and of every longer list up to fourteen.

$5.8M in all. The large money moved another way.

Where the $5.8M landed: 111 Democrats, 84 Republicans, one independent

Gifts from Anthropic’s employees and its PAC together, by the party of the member whose committees received them.

II · The bigger money

Anthropic announced $40.0M for Public First Action. There the trail stops: no filing in this record lists the group’s donors.

What the filings do show: two super PACs the group funds, and $15.0M of independent spending for one House candidate who does not serve in Congress. This record traces no contribution to a specific expenditure.

Source: Anthropic’s announcements; FEC contribution and outside-spending reports of the Public First committees. Not drawn: $1.0M Public First Action passed to a third committee, and one $105K ad naming a member without saying for or against.

The two gifts are as Anthropic announced them; the super PACs reported the spending as independent expenditures. A contribution does not direct spending.

The company’s funders gave more, and for longer.

The 15 candidates the two super PACs spent for or against

Independent spending reported to the FEC in 2026, by the super PAC that spent and the race it named. Four of the 15 now serve in Congress; the spending that named them was all for them.

II · The bigger money

The network’s funders gave more: $170M to outside political groups since 2016, $100M of it from Dustin Moskovitz to one committee.

The 26 committees with network money on record spent $541M on members now serving, from all their donors, $420M of it against Republicans. No dollar is traced from a gift to an expenditure.

Each band is one giver’s money on record; a gift does not direct spending.

Source: FEC contribution and outside-spending reports; BEMC 4 Association’s 2022 IRS filing; Anthropic’s announcements. Not drawn: transfers between the Public First committees, and $4.3M from other individuals, not named.

Of the 26, 24 have gifts on record from the network; two are super PACs that Public First Action funds.

One kind of money reaches more members than any of this, and the network did not give it.

What the 26 committees spent, and what the network gave them

II · The bigger money

No tie reaches more members than lobbyists’ own gifts: 326 received $1.5M from lobbyists at firms with a network client.

For 302 of them a giver is named on that client’s own filings; for the other 24, only the givers’ firms are registered for it. For 83 of the 326, what third parties did is all that ties them to the network: 83 of the 118 such members among the 450 with a tie.

Counted: a gift whose giver was a registered lobbyist at a firm that had a network client in that period. Each lit seat received at least one.

Source: lobbyists’ semi-annual contribution reports to Congress, Feb. 19, 2021 to June 30, 2026; FEC records tie each receiving committee to one member.

The money is the lobbyist’s own, not the client’s, and the record does not say why a gift was made. Named lobbyists only: $1.2M in 1,003 gifts.

That is the lobbyists’ own money. Anthropic’s lobbying is on another record.

Lobbyists’ own gifts to members now serving: who gave, and in which election cycles

74 lobbyists at 23 firms made the 1,162 gifts: 153 Democrats, 172 Republicans and one independent received at least one. The total has grown in each cycle; for 2026, the reports read so far stop at June 30.

III · The lobbying

Anthropic’s reported lobbying spending is up twentyfold since 2023: $280K that year, $5.6M in the first nine months of 2026.

The 2023 sum is what outside firms reported being paid to lobby for Anthropic; the 2026 sum is the lobbying expenses on the company’s own reports, January to September.

Source: quarterly lobbying reports (form LD-2) through Sept. 30, 2026, for Anthropic and the nine other highest-spending network clients in the years drawn; for the share, the 2019–2025 reports this project classified as naming AI or an AI bill by title, after its documented exclusions.

Amounts are as filed, rounded. A quarter with the company’s own report leaves out its outside firms’ reports. A report’s amount covers every issue on it, so 0.5% is a share of report totals, not of AI lobbying; 2025 is the last full year compared.

Small beside the field. But which bills did its reports name?

2025, all network groups together: 0.5% of what was reported on lobbying reports that name AI

2025, all network groups together: $5.6M, the six gold squares among 1,211 (each about $1M, after rounding). On the narrower base, reports whose every issue is AI, their share is 2.9%. 2024–25: Anthropic reported $3.9M, OpenAI $4.8M, Meta $50.7M. January to September 2026, Anthropic alone: $5.6M, the line chart’s number and a different sum. Each report’s amount covers every issue on it, so these are upper bounds on AI lobbying.

III · The lobbying

The three bills most named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic are about chips. All six sponsors received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.

The gifts are separate campaign records: $328,500 in all. None of the specific-issue descriptions on the 68 reports states a position on a bill.

Source: the 68 quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic, 2023 to Sept. 30, 2026 (each bill described from its official title); FEC contribution records.

Naming a bill says the client lobbied on it, not which way and not whether a sponsor’s office was contacted. The gifts are individuals’ own or the PAC’s; no filing in this record ties one to a bill.

How often did a sponsor also receive a gift?

The four bills most named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic

Of the 68 reports filed for Anthropic, 18 name a bill. Each bill is shown with words excerpted from its official title as introduced (Government Publishing Office bill status files), its House and Senate numbers and its sponsors now serving; each dot is one quarterly report that names it, under its year and quarter. Annual defence and spending bills are not ranked (none is named as often as these three); House and Senate versions count as one bill where a report pairs them.

III · The lobbying

Lobbying reports filed for Anthropic name bills by 23 members. 19 of them received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC.

Among the 91 sponsors of AI bills with no bill of theirs named in a network report, it was 47; in all of Congress, 196 of 533. By chamber: 12 of the 13 senators against 60 of all 100, and 7 of the 10 House members against 136 of all 433.

A report that names a bill says the client lobbied on it: not which way, and not whether the sponsor’s office was contacted.

Source: quarterly lobbying reports filed for Anthropic (the company’s own and those of firms it hired), matched to verified sponsors (annual defence and spending bills not counted); AI bills from this project’s companion study; FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

No money is attributed to the lobbying; each gift is an individual’s own or the PAC’s. Which came first, a gift or a report, says nothing about why either was made.

The gifts and the lobbying are recent. Who was Congress hearing from before them?

The 38 members whose bills the network’s lobbying reports name

Filings for Anthropic name bills by 23 members, and 19 of them received a gift from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. Filings for the network’s other groups name bills by 15 more, and 8 of those received one: 27 of 38 with both counted. First the 23 by chamber; then every member by name. Each dot is one quarterly report naming a bill the member sponsored; the bar and the sum are the gifts, all years on record.

IV · The decade before

By the end of 2024, seven of the network’s funders had awarded $528M in grants, and Congress had heard from six of their grantees.

By then, ten of the members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. The grants supported work on AI, technology, biosecurity and catastrophic risk; none of the grants shown names a member of Congress as its recipient.

Source: IRS Form 990 grant schedules and the funders’ own published grant lists; witness lists from congress.gov, House committee pages and Senate hearing transcripts.

A grant to an organisation is not money to a member, and an award is not a payment on its date. Testifying is not lobbying.

Witnesses visit. Who works inside?

The 49 appearances, the grants by year and the 12 largest grantees

Each appearance is at a committee’s invitation. Testifying is not lobbying, and nothing in this record ties a grant to an appearance or to a person.

IV · The decade before

Horizon, a network grantee, has funded 25 fellows inside Congress; 64 people went from Congress to positions with the network or its lobbying firms.

Of the 64, 34 became lobbyists at firms that work for network clients. Horizon says the host manages a fellow’s work.

Each dot is one person.

Source: Horizon Institute placement pages and alumni lists, and its “Host a Fellow” page as saved in 2026; House and Senate payroll reports, lobbyists’ disclosed former posts and organisations’ staff pages; IRS Form 990 grant schedules; for the sheet, FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

A job or a seat is not evidence about the work done in it.

Grants, hearings, fellows, jobs, money. What does that leave on file for each member?

The 20 hosts of Horizon’s fellows, and where the 64 went

Hosts as the programme’s roster lists them, with the year each placement began. Fellows and former staff are counted, not named.

V · The sum

A record of ties, not a record of influence.

The opening slide’s two members again, with what is on file for each: seven kinds of record for Ted Lieu, one for Thom Tillis.

Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026, by party; records through Sept. 30, 2026.

What is on file for all 533 members, and how it was counted

Records through Sept. 30, 2026; independent audits of the latest update were still open on Nov. 26, 2026. The 29 source figures, the tables and the method are in the repository.
